title: What Does It Really Mean to Lead by Example?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The article argues that leading by example is hard because it demands near-perfect consistency, and any deviation or hypocrisy cancels the example's value. It then distinguishes between examples: routine ones like working hard and communicating the vision are presumed of leaders and teach little. The examples that carry disproportionate weight concern how a leader carries himself or herself with others, such as respect, composure under pressure, and openness to challenge. The author's move is to locate the power of example in displayed inner character rather than in processes or habits. The Schweitzer quotation at the end frames example as the only real influence.
points: Leading by example requires near-perfect consistency because a single departure or hypocrisy negates the example.
Team members watch leaders closely, so what leaders do consistently is what gets imitated.
Expected behaviors like hard work and clear communication teach little; the examples that matter most are respect, composure and non-defensiveness.
The strongest example is displayed inner character, more than personal routines or habits.
quotes: Leading by example is exceedingly hard. Not because leaders can’t set a strong example others will follow, but rather because truly leading by example requires near-perfect consistency. Any deviation, exception, hypocrisy, or departure from the example negates whatever made it so worth following to begin with.

A leader who displays and acts with integrity can’t do so 99 percent of the time and still serve as an example. It’s 100 percent or nothing when it comes to illustrating for others what we hope they will emulate.

Team members and colleagues watch leaders like hawks. They zoom in on what leaders do with great consistency and purpose. When they have immense respect for those leaders, they learn from their example.

We presume leaders do some things because they are leaders. They work hard, commit to the team, make sound decisions and communicate openly about the vision, strategy, and goals of the team. Team members rely on these examples but generally don’t take much away from them.

What really matters is how leaders carry themselves and interact with others in various situations. It is that example that speaks the loudest to team members, colleagues, and family members. Leaders who set the example of treating others with respect at all times, maintaining composure (especially under pressure), reacting without defensiveness when challenged, and objectively probing different points of view hold disproportionate weight.

It is the way leaders engage with others that makes the most indelible impression on those around them. While personal processes, routines, and other habits are on the radar for those who observe leaders, it is the example of inner character and how it is displayed that makes leaders worth emulating.
